title: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42)
hook: one sister serves and frets, the other sits at his feet, and one thing is necessary

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Transfiguration: three friends saw him shining. Your line was you can't stay on the mountain. What did you carry down? Day fifty-three. Today, a kitchen.

Something's on the stove, the table isn't set, the bread needs cutting, and there's more to do than time to do it. Guests are here. In Luke's story the guest is Jesus, and a woman named Martha has welcomed him into her home. She's busy with all the serving. And her sister Mary? Mary is sitting on the floor at Jesus's feet, listening. Not helping. Just listening. Martha keeps glancing in, carrying plates, getting hotter by the minute. Finally she walks right into the room and says what she's been thinking. Today: two sisters, and one thing.
screen: `SOMETHING'S ON THE STOVE.` → `MARTHA IN THE KITCHEN.` → `MARY ON THE FLOOR, LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Martha doesn't go to Mary. She goes to Jesus. Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me. It's the same question the disciples asked in the storm: don't you care? And Jesus answers, gently, saying her name twice, the way you speak to someone you love. In the Douay-Rheims: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary. Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." Careful here is old English for full of care: anxious. Luke's word means worry, anxiety. He doesn't say the serving is bad. He's saying: you're anxious about many things, and you're missing the one. And notice where Mary is sitting. At a teacher's feet is a student's place; in Acts, Paul says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. Mary takes the disciple's seat, and Jesus says it won't be taken from her. Some Christian writers, Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas Aquinas among them, read these sisters as two ways of life: the active and the contemplative, doing and praying. But the Church never throws Martha out. She's a saint, with her own feast day, now shared with Mary and their brother Lazarus. And in John's Gospel, it's Martha who makes a bold statement of faith. We'll hear her soon. Monks and nuns try to hold both sisters together: prayer and work, listening and serving.
screen: `LORD, DON'T YOU CARE?` · `MARTHA, MARTHA — ANXIOUS AND TROUBLED.` · `MARY TAKES THE STUDENT'S SEAT.` · `TWO SISTERS, TWO WAYS, ONE HOUSE.` · then, large: `ONE THING IS NECESSARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for two minutes in the middle of a task. You're doing it now, in a way. Settle and breathe. Let the list in your head keep talking; you don't have to answer it. Just notice how many things are pulling at you. Many things. Then let them go quiet for a moment and sit where Mary sat. If you pray, you can just listen. If you don't, listen to the room, to your breath. One thing. The bell holds the time.
Martha and Mary. One sister serving and anxious, one sitting at his feet, and a gentle word about the one thing. Today's word.
Your line: one thing is necessary. Once today, in the middle of something busy, stop for two minutes and just listen. Day fifty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Martha, Mary and Lazarus each July, and religious communities often describe their life as holding Martha's work and Mary's prayer together.

original.note: Greek: you are anxious, you worry. Jesus's word to Martha; the King James and Douay-Rheims say careful.

trapdoor: what you thought: be like Mary, not like Martha.
what it means: serving isn't wrong. Martha is anxious about many things, and Mary has chosen the one that won't be taken away.
what a scholar hears: Mary takes a student's place at a teacher's feet. Augustine and Aquinas read the sisters as the active and the contemplative life.

'In that world, it was usually men who sat that way' (disciples at a teacher's feet): commonly stated; confirm careful phrasing.
Augustine (Sermons 103–104) and Aquinas (ST II-II q.182) on active and contemplative life: confirm references.
